meaning: with all one's strength (heart), resignation, resolution
headline: Omoikiri is the continuative stem of the verb 思い切る (omoikiru).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 思(おも)い切(き)る (omoikiru).

examples.ja: 私は思いきり働きたい。
examples.en: I will work to the best of my ability.

examples.ja: 彼女は彼を思い切りけとばした。
examples.en: She gave him a good kick.

headline: Nemui is related to 眠る (nemuru, “to sleep”), all ultimately related to Classical Japanese 寝 (nu, “to sleep”).

sources.quote: Compare 眠る (nemuru, “to sleep”), 眠り (nemuri, “sleep”), 眠たい (nemutai, “sleepy”), and おねむ (o-nemu, “(childish) sleepiness, sleep”), all ultimately related to Classical Japanese 寝 (nu, “to sleep”, modern 寝る (neru)).

examples.ja: 眠いですか？
examples.en: Are you sleepy?

examples.ja: 今とても眠い。
examples.en: I'm very sleepy now.

headline: Daitōryō is 大 (dai-, “great”) plus 統領 (tōryō, “leader”).

sources.quote: 大(だい) (dai-, “great”) + 統領(とうりょう) (tōryō, “leader”)

examples.ja: 彼は大統領を辞任した。
examples.en: He resigned as president.

examples.ja: 彼は大統領に選ばれた。
examples.en: He was elected president.

headline: Jō, “feelings”, is from Middle Chinese 情.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 情 (MC dzjeng).

examples.ja: 彼女は情にもろい。
examples.en: She is accessible to pity.

examples.ja: 彼は情に厚い人だ。
examples.en: He is a man of warm heart.

headline: Konnichi is from Middle Chinese 今日, the goon reading, so likely the original borrowing.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 今日 (MC kim nyit). Compare modern Taishanese reading gim¹ ngit⁴.
The goon, so likely the original reading of the term as first borrowed from Middle Chinese.

examples.ja: 今日ますます多くの人が、都会より田舎の生活を好むようになっています。
examples.en: Nowadays more and more people prefer country life to city life.

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: Asanebō is 朝 (asa, “morning”) plus 寝坊 (nebō, “sleeping in, waking late; someone who sleeps in”).

morphemes.meaning: sleeping in, waking late; someone who sleeps in

sources.quote: Compound of 朝 (asa, “morning”) + 寝坊 (nebō, “sleeping in, waking late; someone who sleeps in”).

examples.ja: 彼女は朝寝坊だ。
examples.en: She is a late riser.

examples.ja: 朝寝坊が癖になった。
examples.en: I took to sleeping late in the morning.

headline: Shitagi is 下 (shita, “under”) plus 着 (-gi, “clothing”).

sources.quote: 下(した) (shita, “under”) + 着(ぎ) (-gi, “clothing”)

examples.ja: 汚い下着を人前で洗うな。
examples.en: Don't wash your dirty linen in public.

examples.ja: 下着までビショビショです。
examples.en: I got soaked to the skin.

headline: Kaigishitsu is 会議 (kaigi, “meeting”) plus 室 (shitsu, “room”).

sources.quote: 会議(かいぎ) (kaigi, “meeting”) + 室(しつ) (shitsu, “room”)

examples.ja: 会議室は現在使用中です。
examples.en: The meeting room is in use now.

examples.ja: クラブの会員は会議室に集まった。
examples.en: The club members assembled in the meeting room.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Kagaku is Chinese 化學 (huàxué, literally “change + study”), first cited in Japanese in an 1860 translation of a Dutch text.

sources.quote: Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 化學 /化学 (huàxué, literally “change + study”).

Apparently first cited anywhere in an 1855 text in Chinese, in the diary of noted intellectual Wang Tao. First cited in Japanese in an 1860 translation of a Dutch text by 川(かわ)本(もと)幸(こう)民(みん) (Kawamoto Kōmin).
Superseded older term 舎(せい)密(み) (seimi).

headline: Itsu is from Old Japanese, and its first syllable may be a root shared with 如何 (ikaga) and 何処 (izuko).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *Etu. Appears in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.

The presence of other Old Japanese indefinites beginning with い (i) suggests a possible shared root of い (i, possibly “what” or “which”), as in 如何 (ikaga, “how”), 何処 (izuko, “where”), 幾ら (ikura, “how many, how much”).
Likely cognate with eastern Old Japanese word idu (modern idzu or izu, “where”), still used in modern Japanese as part of the word いずれ (izure, “which”).

headline: Hiji is from Old Japanese, first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, from Proto-Japonic *penti.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *penti.

examples.ja: ひじを痛めました。
examples.en: I hurt my elbow.

examples.ja: 彼女は私のひじを引っ張った。
examples.en: She gave a pluck at my elbow.

headline: Kami's kanji 髪 is a shinjitai, simplified from 髮.

sources.quote: Japanese shinjitai. Simplified from 髮 (犮 → 友).

examples.ja: ポールは手で髪を梳きました。
examples.en: Paul ran his hand through his hair.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Subete was originally the -te form of an Old Japanese verb 統ぶ (subu), compare 統べる (suberu).

sources.quote: Originally the -te conjunctive form of Old Japanese verb 統ぶ (subu); compare modern 統べる (suberu, “to gather many things together; to treat many things as a single group”).

examples.ja: 潮の全てはひく。
examples.en: Every tide has its ebb.

examples.ja: 全て嫌いである。
examples.en: I like none of them.

headline: Ii is a shift from 良い (yoi), classical 良し (yoshi), by way of seven steps from yo₂si.

sources.quote: ⟨yo₂si⟩ → */jəsi/ → /joɕi/ → /joki/ → */joɣi/ → /joi/ → */jiː/ → /iː/
Ultimately a shift from 良い (yoi), classical 良し (yoshi).

examples.ja: いい人です。
examples.en: He is nice.

examples.ja: いい塩梅だ。
examples.en: The seasoning is just right.

headline: Kugi is first cited to the Man'yōshu of circa 759 CE, from Proto-Japonic *kunki.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First cited to the Man'yōshu of circa 759 CE, with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 久枳. From Proto-Japonic *kunki.

examples.ja: 板にくぎを打ち込んだ。
examples.en: He hammered nails into the plank.

examples.ja: 彼は板にくぎを打ち込んだ。
examples.en: He drove a nail into the board.

headline: Kamisama is 神 (kami, “deity, god”) plus 様 (-sama, honorific suffix).

sources.quote: From 神(かみ) (kami, “deity, god”) + 様(さま) (-sama, honorific suffix).

examples.ja: 私達は神様を信じます。
examples.en: We believe in God.

examples.ja: あなたは神様を信じますか。
examples.en: Do you believe in God?

meaning: to ridicule, to make fun of
headline: Karakau is attested in The Tale of the Heike (c. 1330); the kara may be cognate with 絡む (karamu, “to become entangled”), and the kau may be 交う (kau, “to exchange; to mix”).

sources.quote: Attested in The Tale of the Heike (c. 1330).

The kara portion is likely cognate with 絡む (karamu, “to become entangled; start a fight with, to pick a quarrel”), 絡める (karameru, “to entangle, to entwine”), and 絡げる (karageru, “to tie together in a sheave or bunch; to hitch up the hem of a robe or skirt”); with an apparent underlying meaning of entanglement, bunch. The kau portion may be 交う (kau, “to exchange; to mix”).

headline: Kakuritsu was coined by Matsumiya Tetsuo in 1908 as a translation of English probability.

sources.quote: Coined by Matsumiya Tetsuo in 1908 as a translation of English probability.

examples.ja: 勝ち負けの確率は五分五分だ。
examples.en: The chances of victory or defeat are even.

examples.ja: 彼が回復する確率はあるにしても極めて少ない。
examples.en: There is little if any hope for his recovery.

meaning: to restrict, to limit, to confine
headline: Kagiru has an uncertain origin: it looks related to 鍵 (kagi, “key”), but Japanese references do not make that connection.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First cited to the Kojiki of 712.
Further derivation is uncertain.

While a surface analysis might suggest a relation to 鍵 (kagi, “key”) or its cognate 鉤 (kagi, “lock”), Japanese references do not make such a connection. In addition, the oldest uses of derived noun 限り (kagiri, “limitation, bound, extent”) indicate that the initial sense was one of "limitation" in terms of time, in contrast to 極み (kiwami, “limitation, bound, extent”) in terms of space.

examples.ja: ハイキングは秋に限る。
examples.en: Autumn is the best season for going on hikes.

examples.ja: 我々は資源が限られている。
examples.en: We have limited resources.

headline: Shiri is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *siri, and its ultimate derivation is unknown.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, in turn from Proto-Japonic *siri. Ultimate derivation unknown.

The use as a suffixing element in surnames is of unclear derivation. Many of these surnames may derive from place names, in which case the "behind, the end" sense may be the origin. However, other surnames have no clear geographic derivation.
From Ainu シㇼ (sir, “place, land, island”). The kanji spelling is an example of ateji.

examples.ja: 頭隠して尻隠さず。
examples.en: Protect yourself at all points.

examples.ja: やめなさい、お尻をぶちますよ。
examples.en: Stop that, or I'll fix your wagon.

headline: Tsuitachi began as tsuki tachi: 月 (“moon; month”) plus 立ち (“standing; starting, occurring”).

sources.quote: /tuki tati/ → /t͡suitat͡ɕi/

Originally a compound of 月 (tsuki, “moon; month”) + 立ち (tachi, “standing; starting, occurring”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 立つ (tatsu, “to stand up; to start, to occur”)).

examples.ja: 四月一日です。
examples.en: It's April first.

headline: Shugi is from Classical Chinese 主義 (zhǔyì), attested in the Records of the Grand Historian.

sources.quote: From Classical Chinese 主義 /主义 (zhǔyì), attested in the Records of the Grand Historian

examples.ja: 彼は完璧主義者だ。
examples.en: He is a person who never cuts corners.

examples.ja: 彼は主義を曲げない。
examples.en: He sticks to his principles.

headline: Tachimachi is apparently a shift from 立ち待ち (tachimachi, “standing and waiting”), first cited in the Man'yōshū of 759.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First cited to the Man'yōshū of 759.

Apparently a shift from 立ち待ち (tachimachi, “standing and waiting”), the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of compound verb 立ち待つ (tachimatsu, “to wait while standing”), probably from the idea of being at the ready. In older texts, this was always followed by the adverbial particle に (ni) for all senses.

headline: Kaku, “to scratch”, is cognate with 書く (kaku, “to write”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kak- (“to scratch”).
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Cognate with 書く (kaku, “to write”).

examples.ja: 大汗をかいた。
examples.en: They sweated gallons.

examples.ja: 彼は赤っ恥をかいた。
examples.en: He covered himself with shame.

headline: Namida is attested as namita in the Nihon Shoki, and later the Man'yōshū has the ta replaced by da.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *namita.

Attested in the Nihon Shoki with the man'yōgana spelling 那(な)瀰(み)多(た) (namita). The Kojiki and Man'yōshū have 那(な)美(み)多(た) (namita), and the Man'yōshū also has later instances where the 多(た) (ta) was replaced with 太(だ) (da), forming 奈(な)美(み)太(だ) (namida), indicating a phonetic change over time from namita to namida.

Ultimate derivation unknown. There are interesting phonetic and semantic similarities with Thai น้ำตา (nám-dtaa, “tear”, literally “water + eye”), overlapping semantically with Korean 눈물 (nunmul, “tear”, literally “eye + water”), perhaps pointing to an ancient prehistoric borrowing. Alexander Vovin lists it among "naturalized loanwords from Korean". However, such similarities may also be purely accidental.

headline: Izure is いづ (izu, interrogative pronoun) plus れ (-re, nominalizing suffix for demonstratives).

sources.quote: /idure/ → /id͡zure/ → /izure/
Compound of いづ (izu, interrogative pronoun) + れ (-re, nominalizing suffix for demonstratives). Long form of いづ (izu).

headline: Yagate contracts 止難 (yamigate): the verb 止む (yamu, “to stop”) plus 難て (gate, “difficult”).

sources.quote: /jamiɡate/ → */jamɡate/ → */jaŋɡate/ → /jaɡate/
Contraction of 止難(やみがて) (yamigate), compound of verb 止(や)む (yamu, “to stop”) + suffix 難(が)て (gate, “difficult”).
First attested around the 10th century.

headline: Jū, “ten”, is from Middle Chinese 十 (MC dzyip), with a literary Hokkien cousin, si̍p.

sources.quote: /ʑipʉ/ → /ʑiɸu/ → /ʑɨu/ → /ʑuː//ʑiʔ/ → /ʑi~̚/
From Middle Chinese 十 (MC dzyip). Compare literary Hokkien 十 (si̍p).

examples.ja: もう夜の十時だ。
examples.en: It's already ten o'clock at night.

examples.ja: 十時半の電車に乗ります。
examples.en: I'm going to take the 10:30 train.
